newsitem.title: USA: U.S. space agency, medical group in research effort.
newsitem.headline: U.S. space agency, medical group in research effort.

text.p: The U.S. space agency NASA and the American Medical Association (AMA) announced on Tuesday a project aimed at enhancing astronauts' health and bringing medical discoveries from space travel to life on Earth.

The two-year project will focus on helping astronauts survive the rigours of long-term stays aboard space stations, especially through techniques of "telemedicine," officials said at an AMA convention.

Telemedicine, in which communications links such as satellite technology and the Internet computer network are used for health monitoring or diagnosis, can have valuable application on Earth as well as in space, medical association president Dr. Daniel Johnson told Reuters.
"The opportunity to apply in inexpensive ways telecommunications technology ... is very promising," Johnson said.

He said telemedicine can be used to bring the expertise of highly trained specialists to patients in rural areas or foreign countries, or for lower-cost monitoring from a patient's home of common medical situations such as heart-surgery recovery or diabetes.
Arnauld Nicogossian, NASA's chief medical officer, told the meeting telemedicine would have a "significant impact on 21st-century medicine."

Under the joint project announced on Tuesday, the two organisations would collaborate on research in medical risks, training in space-based medicine and accreditation of telemedicine techniques used in space.
The two agencies will also share research and planning.

Despite the promise of telemedicine, Tuesday's meeting to announce the collaboration was marred when the sound on an Internet-based link with space medicine experts in Moscow was rendered unintelligible by static and feedback and eventually lost.
Dr. Robert Merrell, a Yale Medical School expert on telemedicine, told the meeting he was undaunted by the glitch.
"I've been victimised by technology most of my career ... and I seem to keep coming back to it, because it gets me places I couldn't go otherwise," he said.
